title: OrganicOasis
subtitle: An indoor hydroponic planter stacked over a kitchen-waste composter
role: Research, testing, concept, industrial design, 3D modelling and rendering
summary: OrganicOasis is an indoor hydroponic planter stacked directly above a kitchen-waste composter, designed in 2023. At the time I was growing plants myself and trying hydroponics, thinking about home hydroponics at an early stage. I wanted to see whether household composting could help hydroponics directly, and whether both could be joined into a small home farm without the smell and mess that usually stop people.

sections.heading: Joining two domestic loops
sections.body:
Composting at home is a green habit, yet in practice it brings odour and easily turns dirty and messy. Home growing runs into its own friction. In a 50-person survey, people started growing vegetables for organic food, lower pesticide worry and steadier supply, then ran into insects, stunted plants, slow growth and small yields.

Mapping two contrasting routines around buying and cooking vegetables showed both ending in the same place, with leftover produce spoiling, food waste building up, and odour and nightly trips downstairs with the garbage following.

sections.heading: Testing smell, breakdown and light
sections.body:
Before drawing a housing, I tested the messy parts directly. A first composting trial with kitchen scraps and compost bacteria ran for seven to eight days and proved slow, leaking water and giving off odour from breaking down proteins. A second three-day test with cut scraps showed that cut thickness and temperature strongly affect decomposition speed.

Alongside that, a 31-day light test compared window daylight against artificial daylight using identical seeds, planting dates and watering. Even moving the plant indoors to follow the sun did not give it enough light to grow quickly. Those trials left six concrete requirements covering finely chopped waste, temperature control, liquid handling, gas filtration, a water cycle and full-time lighting.

sections.heading: Making the structure feasible
sections.body:
A good deal of the project went into structural thinking to make the combined unit as feasible as I could. I chose deep-water hydroponics because it is easier to clean and gives steadier results, housed in modular planting bins that lift out whole for harvesting and washing. Below them, the base packs four systems together, combining rapid composting, a water tank, drying and odour treatment so processed compost and compost liquid return as nutrition for the plants.

I built a cardboard mock-up with a Z-shaped lifting arm, a perforated tray and a base drawer to check bending, reaching and crouching beside the tower. In the finished layout, wet scraps drop into an upper inlet and move down into the composting chamber, folding Z-shaped arms raise the tiers when someone approaches, and slatted light panels on the underside of each tier supply mixed lighting for steady growth.
